items.title: Ownership and moves
items.body: Every Rust value has a single owner, and the value is dropped when its owner goes out of scope. Assigning or passing a non-Copy value moves ownership, and the old binding can no longer be used. This gives deterministic cleanup without a garbage collector.
items.question: Why is let t = s; followed by using s an error for String but fine for i32?
items.answer: i32 implements Copy, so assignment duplicates the bits. String owns a heap buffer; copying just the pointer would create two owners and a double free, so it moves instead. Use s.clone() for an explicit deep copy, or borrow with &s.

source.name: The Rust Book - What Is Ownership?

items.title: Shared XOR mutable
items.question: Why does Rust forbid a &mut reference while any & reference to the same value is still in use?
items.answer: Aliasing combined with mutation causes data races and invalidated references, for example a Vec reallocating while someone holds a pointer into it. Allowing either many shared references or exactly one exclusive reference lets the compiler prove memory safety statically, at zero runtime cost.

source.name: The Rust Book - References and Borrowing

items.title: Borrowing an element, then pushing
items.question: let first = &v[0]; v.push(4); then printing first fails to compile. The code looks harmless. What bug is the compiler preventing?
items.answer: push may reallocate the vector buffer when capacity is exceeded, moving every element to new memory, so first would point into freed memory. The borrow checker sees a shared borrow alive across a mutable one and rejects it. Copy the value (let first = v[0]) or finish using the reference before pushing.

source.name: The Rust Book - Storing Lists of Values with Vectors

items.title: Sharing config across threads
items.question: You need shared ownership of a config object across several threads, with occasional updates. Which types do you reach for?
items.answer: Arc for shared ownership across threads, since Rc is not Send. For mutation add a lock: Arc<RwLock<Config>> or Arc<Mutex<Config>>. For rarely changing config, a Mutex<Arc<Config>> whose inner Arc is cloned by readers keeps lock hold times tiny, and updates swap in a new Arc.

items.title: The ? operator
items.body: The ? operator returns early with the error from a Result (or None from an Option), converting the error type through the From trait. Error propagation stays explicit in function signatures without exceptions.

source.name: The Rust Book - Recoverable Errors with Result

items.title: Send and Sync
items.body: Send means a value can be moved to another thread; Sync means &T can be shared between threads. The compiler derives them automatically from field types, which is why Rc is neither Send nor Sync and RefCell is not Sync, while Arc<Mutex<T>> can be shared.
